intent: Keep the iteration 3 sensing and wheel radius, which produced the oval and s-bend completions, and make the body more agile for the slalom. Reduce mass from 0.6 to 0.5 kg, body_length from 0.14 to 0.12 m, and wheel_track from 0.13 to 0.12 m. Lower yaw inertia should give faster heading response on alternating bends, and the narrower track gives back turn authority. Expected result: slalom progress above 0.34 with some slalom completions, lower max_error on the s-bend, and no loss of oval completions.
learning: Iteration 3 showed that lookahead at y=0.08 m with a 0.04 m wheel converts the oval into completions, but slalom still leaves the line at max_error about 0.064. Next iteration, check: (a) whether slalom max_error drops below 0.06 with the lighter, more agile body, which would confirm yaw inertia is the limit on alternating bends; (b) whether steering_oscillation rises above 0.31, which would mean the agility gain has outrun the damping and the track should return toward 0.13 m; (c) whether oval completion_time falls, which would show the reduced mass has not cost ground speed; (d) whether the s-bend completion rate holds at or above 35%.
rationale:
Iteration 3 is the best design so far (score 503.2). Its three changes (sensors at y=0.08 m, wheel_track 0.13 m, wheel_radius 0.04 m) produced the first real completions: 16 of 20 oval runs and 7 of 20 s-bend runs finished. The slalom still fails in all 20 trials, with progress 0.34 and every run ending off_track. Three signals guide this iteration:

1. Slalom and s-bend fail by leaving the line, not by stalling. Slalom max_error is 0.064, above the 0.06 floor, and s-bend max_error is 0.053, close to it. The robot is not responding quickly enough to alternating bends.
2. Steering oscillation rose slightly (0.31, up from 0.27) and control_effort rose (7.6 to 10.3 on the s-bend), so the controller is working harder without gaining much accuracy.
3. Speed is no longer the constraint on the oval, where completions now happen. The remaining gap is turn agility on tight, alternating curvature.

The wider track (0.13 m) slows the turn response per unit of wheel differential. That helps damping but limits how fast the robot can change heading on the slalom. Yaw inertia is mass*(L^2+W^2)/12. At mass 0.6 kg and L=0.14 m it is about 0.0017. Lowering mass to 0.5 kg and body_length to 0.12 m cuts it to about 0.0011, a roughly 35% reduction, so the same wheel differential turns the robot faster. I am also narrowing wheel_track from 0.13 to 0.12 m, which gives back some turn authority while keeping more damping than the 0.11 m track from iteration 2. Keeping wheel_radius at 0.04 m preserves the ground speed that produced the oval completions. Sensor layout (7 sensors, x = ±0.03 m, y = 0.08 m, 0.012 m footprint) stays unchanged so the Integrator's controller carries over. Body width stays at 0.12 m because the off-track floor of 0.06 m is set by max(0.06, tape_half_width + body_width/4).

Expected result: lower max_error and more progress on the slalom and s-bend, with more s-bend completions. Risk: a lighter, shorter, more agile body may raise steering_oscillation further. If it does, the Integrator will need more kd, and I will then move wheel_track back toward 0.13 m.
